results.pageTitle: Atlas
results.evidenceText: Atlas Atlas digital de desastres no Brasil Mapa interativo Dashboard Downloads Como utilizar Institucional Atlas Digital de desastres no brasil Busque informações sobre os registros de desastres ocorridos no território nacional entre os anos de 1991 e 2025 Acesse o Painel O projeto O que é? É uma ferramenta para análise e consulta das informações relacionadas a desastres no Brasil. Os dados são oficiais da Sedec/MIDR e estão no âmbito municipal. Eles podem ser pesquisados por estados, tipo de desastre e categoria de impacto. Como funciona? É composto basicamente por dois ambientes: o mapa interativo, que gera a visualização espacial dos dados e um resumo dos valores mais significativos; e o dashboard que organiza os dados de ocorrências e perdas em gráficos. Para quem? O Atlas foi desenvolvido para todos os interessados sobre risco e desastres no Brasil, como agentes de Proteção e Defesa Civil nos âmbitos federal, estadual ou municipal, pesquisadores, setor privado e a população em geral. Quem desenvolveu? O Atlas surgiu a partir de uma cooperação técnica entre o Banco Mundial e a Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina, por meio do Centro de Estudos e Pesquisas em Engenharia e Defesa Civil – Ceped/UFSC. Atualmente, a Secretaria Nacional de Proteção e Defesa Civil – Sedec/MIDR mantêm o projeto atualizado, também por meio de parceria com o Ceped/UFSC. Ainda tem dúvidas? Entre em contato conosco por meio de nossa ouvidoria . Official MIDR/Sedec dataset portal. Dataset: Brazilian disaster occurrences, losses and impacts from 1991 to 2024, organized by municipality, state, disaster type and impact category. Format: interactive tables, maps and downloadable data.

results.evidenceText: Buro Media Launches Database of Lukashenko’s Inner Circle | OCCRP Corruption • Belarus Buro Media Launches Database of Lukashenko’s Inner Circle OCCRP’s Belarusian member center Buro Media has launched a database profiling 20 people close to Aleksandr Lukashenko, documenting their assets, business interests, connections, and privileges. Banner: Buro Media | Buro Media’s new database profiles 20 people close to Belarusian leader Aleksandr Lukashenko, documenting their assets, business interests, connections, and privileges. Reported by Aliaksei Hulitski Buro Media November 13, 2026 | 1 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious OCCRP’s Belarusian member center Buro Media has launched Friday a new database, “Favorites,” documenting the wealth, assets, business interests, and connections of people close to Belarusian authoritarian leader Aleksandr Lukashenko. The project currently features 20 profiles, including members of Lukashenko’s family, security officials, businessmen, and public figures. Buro plans to expand the database with additional names. Each profile provides biographical information, details of business activities, and current and historical assets held by the individuals and their associates. The database also documents personal and professional connections, sanctions, criminal proceedings, and privileges granted through ties to Lukashenko, including preferential government loans, tax exemptions, state contracts, and exclusive import and export rights. Several people featured in the database have previously appeared in OCCRP investigations. Viktor Sheiman and Alexander Zingman were linked to a gold-mining deal in Zimbabwe, while Aliaksei Aleksin, Alexander Zaytsev, and Mikalai Varabei were featured in an investigation into Belarusian business networks in Lithuania. The Karić family was also the subject of an OCCRP investigation into lucrative real estate deals in Minsk. Buro Media said the database, current as of November 2026, is intended to help journalists, researchers, diplomats, and analysts better understand the networks of power and wealth surrounding Lukashenko. results.pageTitle: Which fonts to use for your charts and tables | Datawrapper Blog
results.pageDescription: Sans-serif or serif typefaces? Lining or oldstyle figures? Narrow or wide? With lots of examples, we explain which fonts work best for data visualizations.
results.evidenceText: Which fonts to use for your charts and tables | Datawrapper Blog Skip to main content This article is brought to you by Datawrapper , a data visualization tool for creating charts , maps , and tables . Learn more . All Blog Categories How should the text appear in your data visualizations? The possibilities are endless: There are millions of typefaces out there (Arial, Times New Roman, Lato, ...) belonging to different categories (serif, sans-serif, condensed, wide, ...). Many of these typefaces come in different fonts (thin, bold, ...). And then they are so many extra ways of adjusting them (uppercase, size, color, ...). The short answer: When in doubt, set your text in a font that's easy to read. Easy to read is everything that readers are used to. On the web, that means sans-serif , neither overly narrow nor wide , regular (instead of bold or thin) text set in sentence case , in a size that's big enough to read, and in black or almost black. This article explains all these options — and shows how ignoring this advice can set your visualization apart from others. Choosing a font 01 Use sans-serif typefaces. 02 Use a font with lining and tabular numbers. 03 Use a font with all the symbols you need. 04 Use bold fonts only for emphasis. 05 Avoid very thin fonts. 06 Use neither overly narrow nor overly wide fonts. Adjusting the font 07 Use text that's big enough. 08 Use a high-contrast color for most text. 09 Use uppercase text sparingly . Let's start: Choosing a font Use sans-serif typefaces. Serif typefaces (like Times New Roman or Georgia ) bring you into a reading flow — that’s why they’re great for setting long texts like novels or newspaper articles. For data visualizations, sans-serif (”without serifs”) typefaces are most often the better choice. They look cleaner and are often easier to skim than serif fonts, especially when it comes to numbers. Our free Datawrapper visualizations , for example, use the sans-serif typeface Roboto . Changing the fonts – including size, placement, color, etc. – in Datawrapper is possible with a custom theme . Most data visualizations use sans-serif typefaces — like all charts from The Economist and Bloomberg: The Economist, 2022. Fonts: Econ Sans and Econ Sans Condensed. The Economist uses different styles from the same commissioned typeface for all text in their visualizations." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> The Economist, 2022 . Fonts: Econ Sans and Econ Sans Condensed . The Economist uses different styles from the same commissioned typeface for all text in their visualizations. Bloomberg, 2022. Font: Neue Haas Grotesk. Bloomberg's typeface is based on Helvetica but has a slightly straighter appearance, e.g. in its R and a." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> Bloomberg, 2022 . Font: Neue Haas Grotesk . Bloomberg's typeface is based on Helvetica but has a slightly straighter appearance, e.g. in its R and a . While serif typefaces are rare in data vis, they do exist. Serifs look a bit more classy , traditional , and serious/professional than sans-serifs and can set a visualization apart from others out there. Most often, serifs are only used for visualization headlines: The Guardian, 2022. Fonts: Guardian Headline and Guardian Text Sans. The Guardian uses the same commissioned serif font for chart titles as they use for article titles." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> The Guardian, 2022 . Fonts: Guardian Headline and Guardian Text Sans . The Guardian uses the same commissioned serif font for chart titles as they use for article titles. Our World in Data, 2019. Fonts: Playfair Display and Lato. "Display" means the font is only suitable at large sizes, like in titles. (The font name doesn't seem to be an homage to data vis pioneer William Playfair.)" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> Our World in Data, 2019 . Fonts: Playfair Display and Lato . "Display" means the font is only suitable at large sizes, like in titles. (The font name doesn't seem to be an homage to data vis pioneer William Playfair .) The Washington Post, 2022. Fonts: Postoni and Franklin. Like Playfair, Postoni is a Display font: It has a high contrast of thick and thin strokes (just look at that "U" in "Ukraine") and should therefore only be used at large sizes, like here." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> The Washington Post, 2022 . Fonts: Postoni and Franklin. Like Playfair, Postoni is a Display font: It has a high contrast of thick and thin strokes (just look at that "U" in "Ukraine") and should therefore only be used at large sizes, like here. Pew Research, 2022. Fonts: Georgia Italic and Franklin Gothic. Unusual: Pew Research uses sans-serifs everywhere except in the description." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> Pew Research, 2022 . Fonts: Georgia Italic and Franklin Gothic . Unusual: Pew Research uses sans-serifs everywhere except in the description. But some data vis designers use serifs for labels and numbers , too: Federica Fragapane, 2022. Most of Federica's data visualizations use serif fonts. They help set an almost "map-explorative" and literary vibe." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> Federica Fragapane, 2022 . Most of Federica's data visualizations use serif fonts. They help set an almost "map-explorative" and literary vibe. The Guardian, 2018. Fonts: Guardian Text Egyptian and Guardian Figures. One of the rare news projects that uses a serif typeface for all labels and numbers." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> The Guardian, 2018 . Fonts: Guardian Text Egyptian and Guardian Figures . One of the rare news projects that uses a serif typeface for all labels and numbers. If you browse a font catalog like MyFonts , Adobe Fonts , or Google Fonts , you'll notice more categories than just serif and sans-serif: They also let you choose slab serifs , script fonts, handwritten -looking fonts, and monospace fonts. They're all rarely used in data visualization — but here are a few examples: SPIEGEL, 2022. Fonts: SPIEGEL Slab and SPIEGEL Sans. Slab serifs have serifs that are thicker and more emphasized than those of normal serif typefaces." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> SPIEGEL, 2022 . Fonts: SPIEGEL Slab and SPIEGEL Sans . Slab serifs have serifs that are thicker and more emphasized than those of normal serif typefaces. The Pudding, 2020. Font: Walter Turncoat. Handwritten fonts are most often encountered in comics. They give a playful, fictional vibe." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> The Pudding, 2020 . Font: Walter Turncoat . Handwritten fonts are most often encountered in comics. They give a playful, fictional vibe. NBC News, 2022. Font: Founders Grotesk Mono. Monospace fonts give each letter the same width, and hence have a typewriter look and feel." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> NBC News, 2022 . Font: Founders Grotesk Mono . Monospace fonts give each letter the same width, and hence have a typewriter look and feel. Density Design, 2019. Font: Roboto Mono. Another data vis project that uses a monospace." loading="lazy" decoding="async" class=" " style="object-fit:cover;width:100%"/> Density Design, 2019 . Font: Roboto Mono . Another data vis project that uses a monospace. When in doubt, use a sans-serif typeface for the text in your visualization. Roboto , Lato , Open Sans , Source Sans Pro , and Noto Sans are all good options and free to use. None of them will make your visualization stand out, but all of them will be readable and pleasant to look at. If your organization uses a lot of serif text, consider using that same serif typeface for the title of your visualizations to make them more recognizable. 👉 Read more: Choosing Fonts for Your Data Visualization by Tiffany France Use a font with lining and tabular numbers. Different fonts have different ways to display numbers. There are two distinctions: First, between so-called oldstyle figures and lining figures. Lining numbers "line up": They're all the same height. Oldstyle numbers go below and above the "line." They're common in serif typefaces like Georgia and beautiful to look at in a paragraph, but hard to read in a table, tooltip, or as an axis tick. For your data visualizations, use fonts with lining figures. The second distinction is between proportional and tabular figures: Tabular figures are, as the name implies, great for tables. That's because every number is the same width. It's easy to see instantly how many figures a number has, because a 124.17 will be the same length as a 680.90, but shorter than a 1,111.17. So why do proportional figures exist at all, you ask? It's because they're nicer to look at in a paragraph than tabular figures. An 8 deserves more width in text than a 1 , just like a W deserves more space than a J . But for most of your data visualizations, use tabular figures . As in the examples above, oldstyle figures are almost always proportional and tabular figures are always lining figures. All the sans-serif typefaces I mentioned ( Roboto , Lato , Open Sans , Source Sans Pro , and Noto Sans ) come with tabular, lining figures. You can also use font catalogs like Adobe Fonts to filter by "default figure style." 👉 Read more: Finding the best free fonts for numbers by Samantha Zhang 👉 Read more: Fonts for Complex Data by Jonathan Hoefler Do you create a lot of tables and want to go one step further? Then consider fonts with tabular, lining figures that are multiplexed (also called duplexed or uni-width ). Multiplexed means that each character and figure uses the same width in each font weight. Bold text set in most fonts is wider than the same text in a regular font style. Multiplexed fonts don't have that quirk, which makes them great to highlight numbers in tables: To play around with a multiplexed font, you can download and try out Recursive from Google Fonts. For more multiplexed fonts, visit the article Uniwidth typefaces for interface design by Lisa Staudinger. Use a font with all the symbols you need. Besides the figure style, the font you choose should also have all the characters (typographers call them glyphs ) you need. Do you need special characters for specific languages (ü ß é)? Are you using lots of currency symbols ($ € £ ¥)? How about math symbols (+ ÷ × = %)? ® and ©? Reference marks (* † ‡) or superscripts for footnotes (¹ ² ³)? Confirm they all exist before you adjust your whole visualization to a font. All these glyphs need to be drawn by a type designer — often by hand — so don't take for granted that they come with every cheap font. For example, superscript numbers (¹ ² ³) are not simply smaller numbers. Good type designers draw a ² so that it's more legible than a simply size-reduced 2 . Don't just check that all needed glyphs exist, but also that you like how they look . Do the % signs in the Source Code and Recursive fonts make you happy, or are they too experimental for your needs? 👉 Read more: Checklist for choosing data viz typefaces by Diana MacDonald Use bold fonts only for emphasis. Most typefaces come with fonts for different weights , like thin, light, regular (= the default, also called normal), medium (= a slightly bolder regular), bold, and black (= extra bold). Webfonts often use numbers for these weights, where 400 is regular and 700 is bold. Bold or even “black” text feels more self-confident and attention-grabbing than regular font weights. But for the slightly longer text in your visualizations (like descriptions, notes, or annotations) the regular or medium font weights are often the easiest to read. Use bold text only for titles or to emphasize a few words in annotations. Here are two examples, both by The Washington Post: The Washington Post, 2022. Don't use very thin fonts. Text set in a thin or light font weight has such delicate strokes that it looks as if it's set in a brighter color (e.g. gray instead of black). If you're trying to make text look less important while getting around a restrictive color contrast ratio, thinner weights might sound like a great solution. But as you can see in the example above, thin font weights are also really, really hard to read . Only use them in a high-contrast color and in big sizes (often, that means for titles only). 👉 Read more: Do’s and Don’ts of Using Light Typefaces by Anthony Tseng Use neither overly narrow nor overly wide fonts. Narrow (also called condensed) fonts need less space, so it’s tempting to use them in a data visualization. The problem: The less space a character gets, the harder it is to read. Narrow fonts are more difficult to decipher than normal-width fonts. Very wide fonts like Montserrat have the opposite problem: They’re easy to read but use too much space. Most newsrooms use normal-width fonts. I can only think of two that diverge from that norm, NPR and The Wall Street Journal: NPR, 2022. Fonts: Gotham, Knockout, and Helvetica. So far, we covered which typefaces and fonts we should choose for our data visualizations. Let's now talk about how and when we can customize them by making them bigger or smaller, giving them a higher- or lower-contrast color, and making them uppercase. First, the font size: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) have a lot of opinions on how to make the web more accessible and readable. It's likely that your organization tries to comply with these guidelines. So what do they advise your minimum font size to be? Turns out, they don't give a clear answer. That's because the readability of a typeface depends not just on font size, but also on font family, capitalization, letter spacing, and text color : Text annotations in Datawrapper use a default 14px for Roboto. Depending on the font family, everything below 12px will likely be too small. If you're not sure, ask a friend or coworker to help you make the decision. 👉 Read more: Accessible Font Sizing, Explained by Andrés Galante Use a high-contrast color for most text. While the WCAG can't give us a minimum font size, they do mention a minimum contrast ratio . Use a contrast checker to make sure your colors comply. results.evidenceText: Making Internet Things, Part 2: Design Skip to main content How to Make Dope Shit Part 2: Design This is the second installment of a multi-part series designed to help you familiarize yourself with the tools used to make visual, data-driven essays. By Ilia Blinderman Introduction A few months ago, I put together the first part of a guide to help people who wanted to start delving into that hard-to-pin-down brand of storytelling that we do at The Pudding. I was frustrated by the fact that finding sufficiently beginner-friendly resources was so difficult, and decided to collect the most useful links for jumping into data analysis in this blog post . Today, I bring you the second installment of How To Make Dope Shit on The Internet; this one, aimed at helping ease some anxieties that people may have about designing visualizations. Design and Data Visualization Approaching the design of a visualization can be daunting: which insights of your analysis will you visualize? Which chart should you use? How will you code it? The complexity of this chain of decisions can quickly become frustrating. Picking the right way to communicate data may be difficult enough on its own, but pairing it with code, especially when you’re new to programming, can seem exponentially more maddening. I get it — I’ve been there, and that uncertainty sucks. Below, I’ll provide you with a few thoughts on how to make this a little less anxiety-inducing, because at the end of the day, you’re doing cool, exciting work. Look at visualization To learn how to create something, you need to see what others who were practicing it before you were doing. Ernest Hemingway read the works of Shakespeare and Dostoyevsky; Picasso deconstructed the paintings of Velázquez and Goya. While we’re not in the same league, or even playing the same game, the core principle remains the same. In order to know what’s possible — both in terms of what to visualize and how to do it — draw inspiration from past pieces of data visualization that you’ve seen and enjoyed. Internally, we’re always getting excited about work that our peers are putting out. Some of our most consistent sources of inspiration are: The New York Times’ interactives The Upshot The Washington Post Google News Lab The Guardian's interactives The r/dataisbeautiful subreddit I’d also suggest you take some time exploring the archives of Kantar’s Information Is Beautiful Awards , which view like an encyclopedia of some of the best-designed visualizations in the past several years. Another terrific resource is Andy Kirk’s Visualizing Data , which contains a massive monthly archive of his favourite visualizations. Archive the work that you like I frequently come across data viz work that I admire, either due to the clarity of its message, the aesthetic design, or certain subtle touches that solve visual problems I’ve previously struggled to overcome. Since you’re likely to be learning viz on the fly, either while you’re working on a technical project or in your spare time, it’s imperative to keep notes on the most interesting and impressive pieces you encounter. To make sure that I remember the lessons to be gleaned from each of these, I save them to an ever-open Google doc. It’s as simple as taking a screenshot and adding it to the doc with an annotation of what I liked about it, and a link to the original. Another option is to use Sightline , a tool created by Jordan Sechler and Evan Peck, which allows you to automatically save data visualizations you encounter online through a Chrome extension. In addition to automatically compiling your personal archive, you can explore the visualizations that have been saved by other users, which makes trawling for inspiration even easier. Think about your message Before you begin visualizing your data, think through the most important points that you’re trying to communicate. Is the key message the growth of a variable over time? A disparity between quantities? The degree to which a particular value varies? A geographic pattern? Once you have an idea of the essential takeaways you’d like your readers to understand, you can consider which type of visualization would be most effective at expressing it. During this step, I like to think of the pieces of work that I’ve got in my archive and see if any one of those is especially suitable for the task at hand. Other freely available resources are the Data Viz Catalogue or Data Viz Project , which give a long list of chart examples, alongside descriptions of the types of data they’re most suited to. Don’t design in code Once you’ve got a chart in mind, it’s time to design it out. Some people can sketch a few lines on the back of a napkin and jump straight to code, designing as they go (I’m looking at you, Russell ). For most people reading this guide, however, designing on the fly in JavaScript isn’t a viable option: it’s too easy to get bogged down in bugs and syntax, going down StackOverflow rabbit holes rather than designing viz. Instead, I’d recommend spending some time designing the static visualizations using a simpler tool. This will allow you to quickly get a sense of whether or not your visualization communicates the insights you’re hoping to express. There’s no need for coding or fancy software, here. For years, Matt’s been drafting viz in Keynote , and quickly converted me to doing so after we began to work together. It’s surprisingly easy to create data-driven charts and fine-tune their design using Keynote’s in-built capabilities (shapes, masks, gradients, etc.), while keeping the learning curve sufficiently low and avoiding barriers posed by more powerful software like Adobe Illustrator (if you’re comfortable with Illustrator, bless your heart — go forth and design the hell out of your viz, but remember not to get too bogged down in detail). We've also recently started to explore Figma , a web-based design tool that makes it easy to collaborate with multiple team members and helps export CSS styles, and have been thoroughly impressed. Happy with the viz you’ve designed, and itching to make it interactive? Let’s talk code. Ready to learn to code, pt. 1: Read Scott Murray’s Book There are very few resources for learning to code data-driven visualizations that are geared for beginners, and Scott Murray’s Interactive Data Visualization for the Web is one of the few that explains a sufficiently broad range of concepts to get you started with programming. I read his original book cover to cover, and can testify to the fact that it was an incredibly useful resource when it came to helping me understand both general HTML/CSS, and the way that D3, the JavaScript library that we use for data-driven visualizations, works. Moreover, Murray does a terrific job of limiting the concepts he exposes his readers to, which helps beginners bypass the “Dear god there’s so much I don’t understand, EJECT!” stage. I can’t recommend it enough. Ready to learn to code, pt. 2: Look at other people’s code Ian Johnson, known online as enjalot, has created a wonderfully useful tool for browsing data-driven visualizations called Bl.ock Builder . Want to put together a pie chart but aren’t sure how? Just search for “pie” and browse any one of the numerous code examples. Confused by how to use the d3.forceSimulation function? Search for “d3.force” and read through the code — most of the time, you should be able to find a code example that will help you get your head around the tricky concepts. Ready to learn to code, pt. 3: Ask questions! Sometimes, learning how to combine all of these skills can be a lonely endeavour, and it may seem like there’s no one around to help. In truth, the data visualization community is incredibly helpful and supportive. If you get stuck, or just want to talk about coding and visualization with other folks in the same boat, the D3 Slack group can be a great resource. For more pointed technical questions without the camaraderie, posting a question tagged with d3.js posts on StackOverflow is a quick way to clear up any technical ambiguities you’re struggling with. Putting it all together My hope is that the previous sections have helped with any specific design and coding questions you may have faced. Nevertheless, combining all of these steps to create a final output is hard if you’re not used to doing so. That’s why I’d like to leave you with a few examples of the fact that even for pros, design is hard, time-consuming, and iterative. Check out, for example, this image that Scientific American’s Jen Christiansen tweeted out , documenting the numerous design drafts that her team produced to demonstrate the stages of pregnancy: AXS Studio (Contributors: Man-San Ma, Sonya Amin, Eddy Xuan, Joyce Hui, and Susan Park); Jen Christiansen (art direction) The evolution from original concept to final form is dramatic, and I love the fact that Jan, who’s been working at Scientific American for over a decade, puts so much emphasis on honing her team’s designs over a series of steps. Our team has done the same. Consider Matt’s lengthy design process for our collaboration with Google News Lab, examining the diversity in US newsrooms (final project available here ). First, there was the initial whiteboard session: After this, he created a multitude of different designs for the various sections of the project: To see how the final version turned out, head here . Finally, I’d like to leave you with a talk by Mike Bostock, who created the D3 library that we rely on so consistently to produce our visualizations, and who spent several years creating visualizations at the New York Times. Here, he discusses the fact that designing visualizations is a matter of work. While good design may be an innate talent for a select few, most of us are in the same boat: quality work is a function of hours invested, rather than preternatural skill. Seeing the many iterations of Mike’s work is, to me, thoroughly heartening: if someone of his calibre tries a hundred different approaches to see what sticks, it’s a good signal to the rest of us to keep our noses to the grindstone.

Subscribe another address California’s big local news bill becomes law Link latimes.com ↗ Posted by Laura Hazard Owen October 1, 2026 RELATED ARTICLE California legislature passes a major local news funding bill: “If you hire more people, you get more money” Hanaa' Tameez August 31, 2026 At the end of August, the state of California passed a bill to give news organizations tax credits based on the number of journalists they employ. It’s the largest local news bill in the United States — expected to generate as much as $40 million for the state’s newsrooms each year — and on Wednesday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it into law. Assembly Bill 2222, known as the Community Newsroom Employment and Workforce Sustainability Act , gives newsrooms tax credits of $20,000 each for up to five journalists on staff, and $15,000 for every journalist after, as well as $7,500 credits for journalists working part-time and $15,000 new hire credits. The nonprofit Rebuild Local News sponsored the bill. “If you hire more people, you get more money,” Matt Pearce , Rebuild Local News’s director of policy, told Nieman Lab in August. “If you lay people off, you get less money. If you don’t employ anyone, you don’t get anything.” Newsom told reporters that he sees some downsides of the bill, including the fact that it will benefit hedge fund– and billionaire-owned newsrooms. (The guidelines about the types of newsrooms that qualify are here ; the program is “designed to be broadly inclusive.”) From the L.A. Times : While speaking with reporters on Wednesday, Newsom acknowledged some of the concerns that have been raised about those who will receive benefits from the bill’s funds, specifically hedge funds and billionaire owners and outlets that he accused of spreading propaganda. “It does subsidize those that don’t need to be subsidized,” he said. “We have hedge funds in this space. We have billionaires in this space. We have people that are profiteering in this space by gutting the newsrooms and extracting value out of the space that also are the beneficiaries.” Newsom said he chose not to veto the bill because he believes its benefits outweigh the liabilities. He added that he hopes the Legislature and next governor can work to narrow down who benefits most from the legislation. “We should not be subsidizing hedge funds,” he said. “We should be focused on where the need is the greatest, in my humble opinion, and I do think when you have no cap, the limitlessness of this…to some of the most well-heeled organizations, where now they simply could pull from this bill the benefits that they didn’t even ask for or need, is self-evident.” The law goes into effect January 1, 2027, and newsrooms should see credits beginning in 2028. The news company, which launched four years ago , had its first profitable year last year on $40 million in revenue. In a note published Sunday , Smith and Smith said they expect to close the year “substantially bigger” in “revenue and profitability and reach.” RELATED ARTICLE The media startup Semafor launches with a “more honest” article format and lots of global ambition Sarah Scire October 18, 2022 About half of the company’s revenue comes from live events, which Semafor refers to as “convenings.” A two-day convening in November, for example, will cover “Silicon Valley & The World.” The co-chairs include names like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. In their note, the cofounders wrote that “Semafor is starting to emerge clearly as the thing that we hoped it would become.” RELATED ARTICLE Semafor aims to be the source for “intelligent news consumers” who are “unhappy” and “screaming from the rooftops” Sarah Scire September 7, 2022 “We launched with the insight that a leadership audience — CEOs and political leaders alike — was, paradoxically, the most desperate for efficient, fair, and sophisticated news,” they continued. It’s a stretch to say CEOs and political leaders are “desperate” for news. Existing news consumers tend to be older, wealthier, more white collar, and more politically engaged than those who don’t consume news. The genuinely underserved news audiences are elsewhere. Journalism for “decision makers” is one of the most crowded markets in news. Outlets like Bloomberg, Politico Pro, Financial Times, Punchbowl News, Axios Pro, and The Information operate in a similar space. But readers aren’t the primary financial supporters of Semafor’s business. That’d be the corporate sponsors paying for access to its audience through ads and events. Although the annual update says the company has 1.2 million subscriptions, those remain free subscriptions for now. By building a profitable and growing news business, Semafor has done something exceedingly rare. (It now has journalists on the ground in 11 countries and plans to launch in Asia in 2027.) Editor-in-chief Ben Smith explained some of his thinking on an episode of Decoder this summer. In my memory, we always thought at some point we’d do subscriptions, but in my experience you just cannot be ideological about revenue. It’s hard enough to build a business in news without getting all hung up on the values of the different revenue streams. Advertising-based publishers will tell you that democracy can only survive in a world where there aren’t paywalls. Subscription publishers will tell you that advertising is corrupting. At some point you realize everyone’s just talking about their book and that sometimes they’re already in a tough business and they’re talking themselves out of incremental opportunities and really successful media companies. It’s “impossible” for publishers to compete with Google and Meta in the scaled advertising business, Smith told Decoder. He described Semafor as “an anti-scale business.” If you’re reaching people in a very focused way in various particular environments — in person, in email, in video — that’s a case you can really credibly make to advertisers. We’ve built a big advertising and related convening business that way, and that’s one answer. It’s not the only answer, but it is one. The note is here . Subscribe another address Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp. Meta sign at the entrance of the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park, CA. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 15, 2026, 12:59 p.m. Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use. The update , set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab. The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard . As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request. RELATED ARTICLE “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training Sarah Scire September 18, 2026 “This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.” In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products. Here’s the new language about scraping in full: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.” Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.” Meta’s controversial terms October 15 ★ Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann. Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads , and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.” On its developer page , Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access. However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs). Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.” Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode . As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out . Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One . The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service. RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard. “Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.” Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook. Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30. “I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.” Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? results.evidenceText: What to consider when choosing colors for data visualization | Datawrapper Blog Skip to main content This article is brought to you by Datawrapper , a data visualization tool for creating charts , maps , and tables . Learn more . All Blog Categories Data Visualisation can be defined as representing numbers with shapes – and no matter what these shapes look like (areas, lines, dots), they need to have a color. Sometimes colors just make the shapes visible, sometimes they encode data or categories themselves. We’ll focus mostly on the latter in this article. But we’ll also take a general look at colors and what to consider when choosing them: When to use colors in data visualization Consider if there is a better alternative to gradient colors when encoding your most important values.  Gradient colors can be great to show a pattern, e.g. on a choropleth map, but it’s hard to decipher the actual values from them and to see differences between the values. Consider showing your most important values with bars, position (like in a dot plot) or even areas, and to use colors to only show categories. Readers will be able to decipher your values faster: If you need more than seven colors in a chart, consider using another chart type or to group categories together.  Colors make it easy to let readers distinguish between categories in your data, but try to avoid using more than seven of them. The more colors in a chart represent your data, the harder it becomes to read it quickly. Your readers will need to often consult the color key to understand what is shown in your chart. Consider using another chart type: How to make better color choices Consider using the same color for the same variables.  If you just use one color for all your charts, using the same color is the best option to make your article not overly colorful. For example, it’s ok to show the unemployment rate in blue in the first chart and a few paragraphs later a GDP chart with the same color. However, if you use more than one color for your first chart, the colors in this chart will be “taken”. To not confuse readers and increase comparability, consider only using these colors again if you’re showing data about the same category/country/etc.: Make sure to explain to readers what your colors encode.  Every visual mark that represents a value or variable should be explained: What does the height of your bar mean? What does the size of your circles on a symbol map represent? The same is true for colors. There are many ways to create a color key. Here are three of them: Consider the color grey as the most important color in Data Vis.  Using grey for less important elements in your chart makes your highlight colors (which should be reserved for your most important data points) stick out even more. Grey is also helpful for general context data, less important annotations, to show what’s unselected by the user, or to calm down the overall visual impression of your charts. Since grey can seem a bit cold, consider using it with a hint of color: Try a warm grey (grey+yellow/orange/red), or use another very light color as an alternative (e.g. super light yellow): Make sure your contrasts are high enough.  Caring about contrast means caring if your readers will be able to read your chart on their screen, even in low light, and even if you use light colors like grey. This is especially important for text: The smaller the text, the higher its contrast to the background needs to be for it to be readable. The contrast ratio between background and foreground should be at least 2.5 for big text and at least 4 for small text. In addition to having a high contrast ratio, avoid complementary hues (e.g. red and green, orange, and blue) and bright colors for backgrounds. Use  this tool  to test your color contrast, the brightness difference, and if colors are “compliant”. Consider where your colors appear in relation to each other.  The smaller the areas on your chart and the bigger the distance between them, the harder it is to compare them. Consider giving small points or lines a high contrast in their hue or brightness, to make them easily distinguishable. However, big areas can handle toned-down colors with little contrast; especially if there is no other (background)color between these areas: Use intuitive colors.  When choosing a color palette, consider their meaning in the culture of your target audience. If possible, use colors that readers will associate with your data anyway, e.g. party colors: Republican = red, Democrats = blue; natural colors: forest = green, lake = blue; or learned colors: red = attention/stop/bad, green = good (to go). When it comes to color-encoding gender data, consider avoiding the stereotypical pink-blue combination. To not confuse your readers entirely, try a cold color for men (e.g. blue or purple) and a warmer color for women (e.g. yellow, orange or a warm green): Use light colors for low values and dark colors for high values.  When using color gradients, make sure that the bright colors represent low values, while the dark colors represent high values. This will be most intuitive for most readers: Don’t use a gradient color palette for categories and the other way round.  It might be tempting to use shades of one hue (e.g. blue) even for categories, to make your chart look less colorful. However, since many readers will associate dark colors with “more/high” and bright colors with “less/low”, such a color palette will imply a ranking of your categories. Use different hues (green, yellow, pink, etc.) for your categories to avoid that, and to be able to talk about these colors. Readers might be quicker at finding specific categories if you make their colors stand out with a different lightness or saturation, but note that your chart should explain why these colors stand out. If you find your chart too colorful, consider another chart type for your data. Use lightness to build gradients, not just hue.  When designing color gradients, lots of consideration is needed. If you’re unsure, use the defaults of our data visualization tool  Datawrapper , the  ColorBrewer  palettes or these  Carto gradients . If you do want to try your hand at it: Don’t place more than two hues with the same lightness in your gradient, but design it from a bright color (e.g. white) to a dark color (e.g. dark blue) in a consistent way. Your gradient should work in black and white, too. Gradients with much variation in lightness (like rainbow scales) can confuse readers: Consider using two hues for a gradient, not just one.  This is the next step to make your map or chart even more decipherable. Readers will be able to distinguish the colors on the gradient better if they are encoded through lightness  and  (two or three carefully selected) hue: Consider using diverging color gradients.  If you want to emphasize how a variable diverts from a baseline (say the national average), you may want to consider using a diverging palette. It’s important to use clearly distinguishable hues for both sides of the gradient. The center color should ideally be a light grey, not white: Consider color-blind people.  Using different lightnesses in your gradients and color palettes has the big advantage that readers with a color vision deficiency will still be able to distinguish your colors. There are  many  different types of color blindness: Use an  online tool  or  Datawrapper’s automatic colorblind-check  to make sure that color-blind users can distinguish the colors on your chart. To learn more, visit our three-part series on visualizing data for colorblind readers: part 1 , part 2 , part 3 . Want to know more? The Power of The Palette: Why Color is Key in Data Visualization and How to Use It  by Alan Wilson.  Concise but still comprehensive introduction to sequential, diverging and categorial color palettes, with neat illustrations. Subtleties of Color  by Robert Simmon.  Exhaustive introduction to color theory in six parts. Viz Palette for Data Visualization Color  by Elijah Meeks.  Rules for color usage in data visualization that Elijah learned while he and Susie Lu created the tool  Viz Palette , especially in the second part of the article. Make grey your best friend  by Andy Kirk.  Explains all the ways grey is important for data vis. How The Rainbow Color Map Misleads  by Robert Kosara.  Explains the shortcomings of the popular rainbow color scales. Data Stories: Color with Karen Schloss .  Very recent podcast episode about general rules for color usage in data vis, and Karen’s research on the topic in particular. Ask Me Peter Lawson Data and Visualization Librarian Email Me   Contact: Data Services dataservices@jhu.edu Choosing an Appropriate Visual Encoding Data visualization relies on communication through perception . A good data visualization can exploit the natural tendency of the human visual system to recognize structure and patterns. The brain can process information faster and more efficiently when it is in a visual format . Key to achieving this is the choice of visual encodings for your data that correspond to preattentive attributes . Preattentive attributes are visual attributes, including size, color, shape, and position that are processed at a high speed by the visual system. results.evidenceText: How to implement scrollytelling with six different libraries How to implement scrollytelling with six different libraries Russell Samora January 2017 Scrollytelling is the best (or the worst depending on your point of view ). We love it here at The Pudding . But creating a scroll-driven story is hardly a standardized practice, and there are many libraries out there that can help make it happen. Check out my follow-up post , where we look at mobile solutions. “Scrollytelling” is when content (e.g., a graphic) is revealed or changed as the user scrolls. It does not alter scroll behavior, but simply monitors it. As Martha Stewart would say, “It’s a good thing.” Do not confuse this will scrolljacking, which manipulates the browser’s scroll mechanics with JavaScript, which is generally considered bad practice. Here are a few examples of the good stuff in action: In this post, I look at how to tackle a simple scroll-driven chart using six different libraries and share my thoughts on each implementation. It is inspired by Lisa Charlotte Rost’s great post comparing charting libraries. I'm not going to get into the different types of scrollytelling, or debate the serious moral and ethical implications of the practice. I defer to these posts for scrollytelling primers. We want to make something like this: There are two goals here: 1. Use the "scroll-to-trigger" pattern where the trigger element (in our case a block of text) tells the chart to update to a new state. 2. We want the chart to stay fixed while the text moves and have it snap back into place as it enters and exits, because often the scrollytelling portion is not the entire story. Disclaimer: this post does not cover responsive solutions (though you should do it, and most libraries make it pretty painless). If you have the audacity to resize your browser, refresh the page. For mobile and responsive solutions, check out my follow-up post, Update (November 2017): I created my own scrollytelling library, scrollama.js . The goal of this library is to provide a simple interface for creating scroll-driven interactives. Scrollama is focused on perfomance by using IntersectionObserver in favor of scroll events. Check it out . #1 - Waypoints Waypoints is a very solid choice. It has been around for a while, and supports both vanilla JS and jQuery integration. It has an easy to understand API, and good documentation. It has a lot of add-ons, like a debugger extension to reduce some head-scratching, inview detection, and sticky elements. Below is the core code used to implement this library. See the demo for the full code with comments. Subscribe another address How a plan to turn the Spokane Spokesman-Review into “The People’s Paper” ended in a newsroom revolt Newsroom staffers say that concerns about Rob Curley’s leadership festered until his August suspension — weeks before the paper was set to transfer to his nonprofit. Rob Curley, executive editor of the Spokesman-Review in Spokane, Washington, speaking at the 2023 News Media Mega-Conference. (scottcornelius.com ) By Wilson Criscione, InvestigateWest and Daisy Zavala Magaña, RANGE Oct. 5, 2026, 2:44 p.m. This report was produced in a collaboration between InvestigateWest and RANGE . When the Spokesman-Review announced plans to transfer Spokane’s 143-year-old, family-owned newspaper to a nonprofit founded by executive editor Rob Curley, it took over the front page. “The People’s Paper,” read the April 16, 2025, headline, saying ownership would transfer “to you, the community.” Key to the plan was Curley, the folksy self-proclaimed “journalism nerd” who burst into Spokane a decade ago, declaring a love for Gonzaga University basketball rivaled only by his love for Disney. The transition to Comma Community Journalism Lab was cast in media industry publications not only as a way to save Spokane’s daily newspaper, but as part of a growing movement to resurrect dying papers by making them less dependent on ads and corporate ownership and more on philanthropy and community partnerships. As proof of concept, the paper had already added several so-called “community-funded” journalists to its staff. But in the Spokesman-Review newsroom this summer, that hopeful vision ran into persistent concerns about Curley’s leadership. More than a dozen current and former employees, along with contemporaneous records reviewed by InvestigateWest and RANGE, reveal how the newsroom had raised concerns about Curley’s management for years, culminating in his suspension from the paper on Aug. 7 and a vote of no confidence from the union, the Spokane Editorial Society. He is currently on leave as the paper conducts an internal investigation. Employees said stories that might have angered powerful community figures or potential donors were killed or curtailed, and that they felt he retaliated against workers he viewed as disloyal. Staffers questioned his financial oversight of Comma, which hired his own son at a salary topping most reporters’ and recruited out-of-town executives to serve as top editors before Comma had met its fundraising goal. Current and former Spokesman-Review employees also described workplace complaints involving Curley and one of those editors, including allegations of inappropriate lewd and sexual comments around employees, including teenage interns. Curley declined to comment for this article. In a brief phone interview, Curley’s attorney, Patrick Kirby, who specializes in employment and wrongful termination cases, said, “It’s all inaccurate,” in reference to a list of claims InvestigateWest and RANGE provided to Curley prior to publication. Kirby hung up the call when a reporter pressed him on which claims specifically he believed were inaccurate. The top of Page 1 of The Spokesman-Review, April 16, 2025. Tensions in the newsroom came to a head in the first week of August, as the paper rallied to cover the most destructive wildfires in Spokane’s history and the imminent ownership transfer approached at the end of the month. Some staffers were alarmed at the prospect of working for an organization Curley founded, with even fewer checks on his authority. “The terror had been building through advertising, circulation, and this newsroom each day, getting closer to the day of knowing we would have to work for Rob without the filter of human resources and the publisher,” said one employee, speaking anonymously for fear of retribution. Reporters had grown increasingly frustrated with Comma editors meddling with stories, and Curley tried to fire a reporter who pushed back, employees say. But instead, when other Spokesman-Review editors backed the reporter, publisher William “Stacey” Cowles suspended Curley, citing “ several personnel complaints ” against him. It wasn’t until after Curley’s suspension that reporters were told news that called the Comma plan into question. In a meeting days after Curley had been kicked out of the building, Spokesman-Review management shared that despite public claims by Curley that several reporters were paid for by community donors — a source of optimism for the Comma plan — none of the paper’s reporting positions were currently community-funded. There were “audible gasps,” according to several reporters in the room. The paper had been promoting its community-funded reporters online, removing paywalls for stories written by those journalists. One reporter remembered how at fundraising events, Curley would point to a journalist’s face on a big screen and tell donors that their money paid for journalists’ salaries. Even the reporters took pride in sharing the claim with readers. “I’ve been lying on his behalf without even knowing it,” one reporter said. Cowles, the publisher, said he had no comment on the claims about Curley until the conclusion of the internal investigation. He said the paper is targeting Oct. 30 to close the transaction with Comma. Bill Simer, Comma Community Journalism Lab board chair, did not comment for this article. Saving local journalism Before joining the Spokesman-Review in 2016, Curley had been praised in some journalism circles as a leader in transitioning struggling newspapers away from print and into the digital world. In naming Curley as the Spokesman-Review’s new top editor, Cowles said Curley had “a proven record of delivering news that matters” and that his “innovative work” at previous newspapers helped them win top journalism awards “including a Pulitzer Prize,” the announcement said. But reporters at his previous gigs viewed him differently : as a mercurial leader who hyped expensive, ineffective initiatives, sacrificing journalism ethics to keep up cozy relationships with powerful community institutions and politicians. The Orange County Register in Southern California was criticized for favorable coverage of Disney under Curley, who served as the paper’s top editor between 2014 and 2016 and proudly said he wore a Mickey Mouse garment every day. He also faced backlash when he revised an article two months after it had been published at the request of a politician, despite police reports and other records that didn’t support the change . Curley changed the story over the objections of the reporter and did not note the changes for the public with a correction or editor’s note — a decision journalism ethicists called an “unethical overreach.” Journalists from the Las Vegas Sun in Nevada had their own problems with him. After he left the Sun in 2012, they noticed that Curley kept getting credit for the paper’s Pulitzer Prize in 2009 — credit that Cowles repeated in the 2016 hiring announcement. Sun employees clarified to the Inlander, a Spokane alt-weekly, that Curley, in fact, had nothing to do with the series that won the Pulitzer. Curley said he’d never told anyone he won a Pulitzer, blaming a series of misunderstandings for it showing up time and time again in his biography. Curley stuck around Spokane, undaunted by the controversies from his past. And with layoffs and buyouts shrinking the newsroom in a struggling industry, Curley two years ago began testing the Comma pitch among staff by signaling that it would save their jobs. Reporters said he told them privately that they’d receive big raises once the transfer happened. If Comma didn’t move forward, he said the Cowles family would likely lay off staff or maybe sell the locally owned paper to one of the hedge fund–owned companies known for downsizing newsrooms, one current employee recalled. Reporters felt Curley had compromised editorial independence at the Spokesman as well. Staffers took issue with Curley altering an article in 2025 about a bond proposal from Spokane Public Schools. In the article, reporters wrote a passage explaining how the proposal could raise property taxes. The story had been cleared by the typical story editors, but late the night before the story was published, Curley had a copy editor change that passage “to be more in line with what the school district wanted us to be saying,” said Emry Dinman, one of the article’s two reporters. “My editors were all as outraged as I was.” Staffers knew Comma was trying to partner with the school district as part of the ownership transition, though Dinman said he didn’t want to speculate on the intentions behind the late-night edit. Current and former staffers also said Curley didn’t like articles that were critical of Gonzaga, a private university downtown most known for its basketball team that Curley frequently celebrated in his columns. Rebecca Hansen-White, a former reporter at the Spokesman-Review from 2018 to 2020, said that during the COVID-19 pandemic she wrote a story about Gonzaga’s plans for an isolation facility, which included some light criticism from a local politician for the private university using government money to do so. But the story was never published. When Hansen-White asked what happened, she recalls an editor told her something to the effect of “that may have been one Rob didn’t want to run,” though she was never able to confirm if Curley spiked it himself. “That was very frustrating. I worked hard on this and I’m going out to the community and I’m getting in these tough conversations with sources,” she said. “And then I come back to the newsroom and find that my work has been changed or removed without an explanation.” Comma eventually set up shop on the Gonzaga campus in 2024 . The two editors who Curley hired for Comma in fall 2025 did little to ease reporter concerns about outside interference. Donna Wares and Ron Sylvester had both worked with Curley at the Orange County Register, and when Curley brought them into the Spokesman-Review newsroom, an email sent to the staff described their roles until the transfer as “consultants” — Sylvester for “newsroom metrics and trust initiatives,” and Wares for “enterprise story assignment, editing and Northwest Passages author recruitment.” Northwest Passages is the nonprofit’s book club and event series. That distinction was crucial for Spokesman-Review staffers, who considered it a breach of journalistic integrity to have non-staffers weigh in on editorial decisions, even if it came from people who would one day be their editors. “We were told through the union that Comma editors would not be able to touch our stories until the transition happened,” said Emily White, a former reporter who left the Spokesman at the end of August. But that’s not what happened. “They were tampering with our stories with no permission,” White said. The union filed a grievance with the company, said Thomas Clouse, union president and longtime reporter. “Our understanding was that the publisher dealt with it,” he said. A newsroom altercation As Comma took longer than initially expected to reach its $2 million fundraising goal, the transition kept being delayed. The presence of Comma staff in the newsroom, meanwhile, grew louder. Comma had also hired one of Curley’s sons. Johnathan Curley made a salary of $62,400, according to a 2025 court document, topping the pay of almost every Spokesman-Review reporter. His title at Comma is “technical director,” and he handles video and audio equipment for Comma events. Previously, the 24-year-old worked as a part-time audio-visual technician for Cirque du Soleil in Las Vegas. Johnathan Curley did not respond to requests for comment. Staffers questioned how much Sylvester and Wares were getting paid to be Comma editors before the transition, and they were concerned that Wares spent half her time in California, flying back and forth on Comma’s dime. Sylvester lingered in the newsroom, with staff increasingly unclear of his role. Employees described Sylvester as a disorganized and unproductive editor who often shopped online for magician supplies while in the office. He was tasked with managing the summer internship program, they said, but his involvement was so marginal that other staff had to pick up his slack. “If you ask what his job entailed, I wouldn’t be able to give you an answer,” one staffer said. Sylvester did not respond to requests for comment. In early August, with the planned transition to Comma just weeks away, the newsroom scrambled to cover wildfires that had caught national attention. The staff worked day and night, eventually breaking the news that one of the blazes was set by an arsonist. Courts reporter Alexandra Duggan, as it turned out, had been one of the first people to see the alleged arsonist near the flames. The Review Building, which houses the Spokesman-Review office, in downtown Spokane, Washington on September 30, 2026. (Wilson Criscione/InvestigateWest) On Aug. 4, Sylvester told reporters they should change how they attribute documents in stories. Instead of citing “court documents,” he said they should cite “sworn affidavits.” Despite having no clear editorial role in the Spokesman-Review newsroom, Sylvester went into Duggan’s story that night and made a change reflecting his preference — except in that instance, the record was not in fact an affidavit. It introduced an error into the paper. Clouse, the union president, said he called a meeting with management to try to understand why Comma editors were meddling with stories again. “That never got resolved,” he said. Two days later, Duggan, who’d worked 13 straight days, was finishing up another story about the accused arsonist. Sylvester approached her and said, in a low voice, “you’re doing it again,” several employees who witnessed or learned of the altercation told InvestigateWest and RANGE. He’d been referring to her story saying “court documents.” Duggan walked away. But Sylvester followed, and the two shouted back and forth at each other until other editors stepped in to cool things down. “I wanted to make sure that our stories were truthful and honest and that they were not being edited without us knowing and without any communication,” Duggan said. “And I just wanted to keep the integrity of the paper.” Curley sided with Sylvester, telling Spokesman-Review managing editor Lindsey Treffry that night to fire Duggan. Treffry refused. The next morning, during a series of meetings with Cowles, Treffry and other editors shared complaints they had about Curley. Cowles decided to put Curley on administrative leave, revoking his keycard access to the paper’s offices. A few hours later, however, Curley got in the newsroom again by asking an unsuspecting intern for their keycard. He walked around asking where he could find Treffry, who, according to several staffers there that day, was hiding from Curley in the photo room with other editors. Duggan joined them, and it was there that Duggan learned Treffry saved her job. As they hid, Duggan texted White, who was not in the newsroom at the time. White shared the texts with InvestigateWest and RANGE that described how an HR employee escorted Curley out of the building. “They chased Rob out of the newsroom,” Duggan texted. “I can’t see because I’m hiding.” “I’m hysterical,” Duggan wrote, crumpled into a ball and crying. Duggan said she’d “ride or die for this paper.” She said Curley’s attempt to fire her “felt like a slap in the face — it felt like betrayal.” In an interview for this story, she said she’ll be grateful for the rest of her life that Treffry had her back. “She did save my job. And she protected the rest of us from something similar,” Duggan said. “Jessica Rabbit” Former reporter Rachel Alexander, who worked at the Spokesman-Review from October 2014 to July 2018, recalled a pattern of “cronyism and ethics violations.” In a letter she sent to investigators after Curley’s suspension, Alexander described a departure of women on staff and in leadership roles during Curley’s first year; editors who left meetings with him looking “shaken, exhausted and at times afraid”; and how Curley didn’t keep promises to sponsor a former staff member’s work visa if he left the union. “Despite the meaningful journalism I was able to do and the presence of many talented colleagues who I greatly admire, I could not in good conscience continue working for a man who was willing to lie to a friend and jeopardize his ability to remain in the country,” Alexander wrote. “I made the decision to leave the Spokesman in 2018 primarily because of Mr. Curley’s behavior.” Before leaving, Alexander noticed that she was “nearly the only woman left on the desk,” according to her letter. She also told investigators that Curley seemed to primarily “take issue with or pick fights” with women in the newsroom. Instead of talking through concerns, he made “petty” decisions, like blocking reporters on Twitter, she wrote. In recent years, the paper has hosted high school interns as part of Curley’s effort to make Comma into a training ground for young journalists. But the behavior of Curley and Sylvester made some employees question whether they should be responsible for mentoring young journalists. One letter shared with internal investigators described how, during a 2024 barbecue for Spokesman-Review interns at Curley’s house, two teenage interns saw sexually explicit images of women on Curley’s iPad as he scrolled through his camera roll. Curley had been giving the high school girls a tour of his home and showing off his guitar collection. He was looking for song lyrics on his iPad when the inappropriate pictures flashed on his screen, according to employees who had heard of the incident from the interns. Several staff members also brought concerns to HR about inappropriate comments Sylvester made around interns who were in high school and college. In a conversation with another employee about the evolution of photography — and while sitting near an 18-year-old intern — Sylvester joked that if someone wanted to send a “dick pic” back in the day, they had to wait for it to develop, but today it can be done in an instant. On a different occasion, Sylvester told another employee to wait a few seconds before downloading porn, according to several employees. It was loud enough for other employees to hear the unprompted comment, including nearby interns. “It was very shocking to hear someone … who was supposed to be a mentor figure say that,” a staffer who witnessed the exchange said. “It’s just not appropriate for the workplace.” Current and former staff members also described a work environment where people perceived as being against Curley or who reported issues to HR were retaliated against. They felt Curley had favorites — including Sylvester and Wares — who would not face consequences for their actions. After an employee reported Sylvester to HR for his comment about dick pics, a letter to investigators said Curley appeared to retaliate against those he believed had made the report. Curley excluded one of the employees from important meetings and avoided another employee and gave them “distasteful looks.” Curley needed to make sure staff was “loyal” to him, employees said. Google’s News AI pilot expands to over 400 publications, including U.S. local news outlets Link blog.google ↗ Posted by Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 In December, Google launched its News AI pilot program, which licenses content from select publishers and uses it to test new AI features in Google News. On Thursday, the company announced that the program has added new partnerships, bringing the total number of publications in the pilot to more than 400 worldwide. At launch, the program partnered with international publishers like The Guardian, El País, The Times of India, and The Washington Post. More publications are now coming on board, including CNN, The Financial Times, Axios, and Forbes. RELATED ARTICLE Discover isn’t the only place Google is experimenting with AI-generated snippets Andrew Deck January 26, 2026 As part of the expansion, the program has also added local news publishers across the U.S., including The Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina; Oil City News in Casper, Wyoming; the Illinois- and Iowa-based newspaper chain Shaw Media ; and the nonprofit newsroom The Texas Tribune . “People’s information consumption habits are changing, and we want to make sure publishers of all sizes, local newsrooms included, can navigate these shifts,” Brianna Puccini Duff, a spokesperson for Google, said in a statement to Nieman Lab. Google declined to comment on the exact terms of the deals. However, Duff clarified that the News AI pilot does not operate on a “ pay-per-value ” model, meaning publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to an AI-generated output. (The pay-per-value model is part of a parallel program that pays publishers for content surfaced in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and Gemini, according to a recent report by Digiday .) With the News AI pilot, publishers are instead paid to provide content that appears in experimental AI-powered features. That includes “story previews” — in-depth, AI-generated article summaries of recent stories that may show up on a publisher’s Google News page. Here’s a Washington Post example, with a disclaimer noting the copy is AI-generated and “may include mistakes.” An AI-generated “story preview” on the Google News page for The Washington Post Another test feature is “audio briefing,” a customizable, AI-generated podcast in the Google News app that stitches together daily headlines.
