Subscribe another address From bad to worse: 2026 is shaping up to be “a super El Niño year for local news” Link localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu ↗ Posted by Sophie Culpepper October 13, 2026 RELATED ARTICLE In Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than ever Sophie Culpepper October 22, 2025 If you thought last year was bleak , Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder. What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin , founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.” In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged. Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report. “When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states. RELATED ARTICLE Last year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s going Sophie Culpepper February 9, 2026 Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024. “Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois . “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.” The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left. A few other highlights from this year’s report: The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas. Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022. Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit . The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms. Read more in the full report here . Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap: Center of Excellence Feedback Summarize this article for me Note This article forms part of the Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap series of articles. For an overview of the series, see Microsoft Fabric adoption roadmap . A data or analytics Center of Excellence (COE) is an internal team of technical and business experts. The team actively assists others within the organization who are working with data. The COE forms the nucleus of the broader community to advance adoption goals, which align with the data culture vision. A COE might also be known as competency center , capability center , or a center of expertise . Some organizations use the term squad . Many organizations perform the COE responsibilities within their data, analytics, or business intelligence (BI) team. Note Having a COE team formally recognized in your organizational chart is recommended, but not required. What's most important is that the COE roles and responsibilities are identified, prioritized, and assigned. It's common for a centralized data or analytics team to take on many of the COE responsibilities; some responsibilities might also reside within IT. For simplicity, in this series of articles, COE means a specific group of people , although you might implement it differently. It's also very common to implement the COE with a scope broader than Fabric or Power BI alone: for instance, a Power Platform COE, a data COE, or an analytics COE. Goals for a COE Goals for a COE include: Evangelizing a data-driven culture. Promoting the adoption of analytics. Nurturing, mentoring, guiding, and educating internal users to increase their skills and level of self-reliance. Coordinating efforts and disseminating knowledge across organizational boundaries. Creating consistency and transparency for the user community, which reduces friction and pain points related to finding relevant data and analytics content. Maximizing the benefits of self-service BI, while reducing the risks. Reducing technical debt by helping users make good decisions that increase consistency and result in fewer inefficiencies. Important One of the most powerful aspects of a COE is the cross-departmental insight into how analytics tools like Fabric are used by the organization. This insight can reveal which practices work well and which don't, that can facilitate a bottom-up approach to governance. A primary goal of the COE is to learn which practices work well, share that knowledge more broadly, and replicate best practices across the organization. Scope of COE responsibilities The scope of COE responsibilities can vary significantly between organizations. In a way, a COE can be thought of as a consultancy service because its members routinely provide expert advice to the internal community of users. To varying degrees, most COEs handle hands-on work too. Common COE responsibilities include: Mentoring and facilitating knowledge sharing within the internal Fabric community. Holding office hours to engage with the internal Fabric community. Conducting co-development projects and best practices reviews in order to actively help business units deliver solutions. Managing the centralized portal . Producing, curating, and promoting training materials . Creating documentation and other resources, such as template files , to encourage consistent use of standards and best practices. Applying, communicating, and assisting with governance guidelines. Handling and assisting with system oversight and Fabric administration. Responding to user support issues escalated from the help desk. Developing solutions and/or proofs of concept. Establishing and maintaining the BI platform and data architecture. Communicating regularly with the internal community of users. Staffing a COE People who are good candidates as COE members tend to be those who: Understand the analytics vision for the organization. Have a desire to continually improve analytics practices for the organization. Have a deep interest in, and expertise with, analytics tools such as Fabric. Are interested in seeing Fabric used effectively and adopted successfully throughout the organization. Take the initiative to continually learn, adapt, and grow. Readily share their knowledge with others. Are interested in repeatable processes, standardization, and governance with a focus on user enablement. Are hyper-focused on collaboration with others. Are comfortable working in an agile fashion. Have an inherent interest in being involved and helping others. Can effectively translate business needs into solutions. Communicate well with both technical and business colleagues. Tip If you have self-service content creators in your organization who constantly push the boundaries of what can be done, they might be a great candidate to become a recognized champion , or perhaps even a satellite member of the COE. When recruiting for the COE, it's important to have a mix of complementary analytical skills, technical skills, and business skills. Roles and responsibilities Very generalized roles within a COE are listed below. It's common for multiple people to overlap roles, which is useful from a backup and cross-training perspective. It's also common for the same person to serve multiple roles. For instance, most COE members also serve as a coach or mentor. Role Description COE leader Manages the day-to-day operations of the COE. Interacts with the executive sponsor and other organizational teams, such as the data governance board, as necessary. For an overview of additional roles and responsibilities, see the Governance article. Coach Coaches and educates others on data and BI skills via office hours (community engagement), best practices reviews , or co-development projects . Oversees and participates in the discussion channel of the internal community. Interacts with, and supports, the champions network . Trainer Develops, curates, and delivers internal training materials, documentation, and resources. Data analyst Domain-specific subject matter expert. Acts as a liaison between the COE and the business unit. Content creator for the business unit. Assists with content certification. Works on co-development projects and proofs of concept. Data modeler Creates and manages data assets (such as shared semantic model and dataflows (legacy)) to support other self-service content creators. Report creator Creates and publishes reports, dashboards, and metrics. Data engineer Plans for deployment and architecture, including integration with other services and data platforms. Publishes data assets which are utilized broadly across the organization (such as a lakehouse, data warehouse, data pipeline, dataflow, or semantic model). User support Assists with the resolution of data discrepancies and escalated help desk support issues. As mentioned previously, the scope of responsibilities for a COE can vary significantly between organizations. Therefore, the roles found for COE members can vary too. Structuring a COE The selected COE structure can vary among organizations. It's also possible for multiple structures to exist inside of a single large organization. That's particularly true when there are subsidiaries or when acquisitions have occurred. Note The following terms might differ to those defined for your organization, particularly the meaning of federated , which tends to have many different IT-related meanings. Centralized COE A centralized COE comprises a single shared services team. Pros : There's a single point of accountability for a single team that manages standards, best practices, and delivery end-to-end. The COE is one group from an organizational chart perspective. It's easy to start with this approach and then evolve to the unified or federated model over time. Cons : A centralized team might have an authoritarian tendency to favor one-size-fits-all decisions that don't always work well for all business units. There can be a tendency to prefer IT skills over business skills. Due to the centralized nature, it might be more difficult for the COE members to sufficiently understand the needs of all business units. Unified COE A unified COE is a single, centralized, shared services team that has been expanded to include embedded team members. The embedded team members are dedicated to supporting a specific functional area or business unit. Pros : There's a single point of accountability for a single team that includes cross-functional involvement from the embedded COE team members. The embedded COE team members are assigned to various areas of the business. The COE is one group from an organizational chart perspective. The COE understands the needs of business units more deeply due to dedicated members with domain expertise. Cons : The embedded COE team members, who are dedicated to a specific business unit, have a different organizational chart responsibility than the people they serve directly within the business unit. The organizational structure could potentially lead to complications, differences in priorities, or necessitate the involvement of the executive sponsor. Preferably, the executive sponsor has a scope of authority that includes the COE and all involved business units to help resolve conflicts. Federated COE A federated COE comprises a shared services team (the core COE members) plus satellite members from each functional area or major business unit. A federated team works in coordination, even though its members reside in different business units. Typically, satellite members are primarily focused on development activities to support their business unit while the shared services personnel support the entire community. Pros : There's cross-functional involvement from satellite COE members who represent their specific functional area and have domain expertise. There's a balance of centralized and decentralized representation across the core and satellite COE members. When distributed data ownership situations exist—as could be the case when business units take direct responsibility for data management activities—this model is effective. Cons : Since core and satellite members span organizational boundaries, the federated COE approach requires strong leadership, excellent communication, robust project management, and ultra-clear expectations. There's a higher risk of encountering competing priorities due to the federated structure. This approach typically involves part-time people and/or dotted line organizational chart accountability that can introduce competing time pressures. Tip Some organizations have success by using a rotational program . It involves federated members joining the core COE for a period of time, such as six months. This type of program allows federated members to learn best practices and understand more deeply how and why things are done. Although each federated member remains focused on their specific business unit, they gain a deeper understanding of the organization's challenges. This deeper understanding leads to a more productive partnership over time. Decentralized COE Decentralized COEs are independently managed by business units. Pros : A specialized data culture exists that's focused on the business unit, making it easier to learn quickly and adapt. Policies and practices are tailored to each business unit. Agility, flexibility, and priorities are focused on the individual business unit. Cons : There's a risk that decentralized COEs operate in isolation. As a result, they might not share best practices and lessons learned outside of their business unit. Collaboration with a centralized team might be informal and/or inconsistent. Inconsistent policies are created and applied across business units. It's difficult to scale a decentralized model. There's potential rework to bring one or more decentralized COEs in alignment with organizational-wide policies. Larger business units with significant funding might have more resources available to them, which might not serve cost optimization goals from an organizational-wide perspective. Important A highly centralized COE tends to be more authoritarian , while highly decentralized COEs tend to be more siloed . Each organization will need to weigh the pros and cons that apply to them to determine the best choice. For most organizations, the most effective approach tends to be the unified or federated, which bridges organizational boundaries. Funding the COE The COE might obtain its operating budget in multiple ways: Cost center. Profit center with project budget(s). A combination of cost center and profit center. When the COE operates as a cost center, it absorbs the operating costs. Generally, it involves an approved annual budget. Sometimes this is called a push engagement model. When the COE operates as a profit center (for at least part of its budget), it could accept projects throughout the year based on funding from other business units. Sometimes this is called a pull engagement model. Funding is important because it impacts the way the COE communicates and engages with the internal community. As the COE experiences more and more successes, they might receive more requests from business units for help. It's especially the case as awareness grows throughout the organization. Tip The choice of funding model can determine how the COE actively grows its influence and ability to help. The funding model can also have a big impact on where authority resides and how decision-making works. Further, it impacts the types of services a COE can offer, such as co-development projects and/or best practices reviews. For more information, see the Mentoring and user enablement article. Some organizations cover the COE operating costs with chargebacks to business units based on the usage goals of Fabric. For a shared capacity, this could be based on number of active users. For Premium capacity, chargebacks could be allocated based on which business units are using the capacity. Ideally, chargebacks are directly correlated to the business value gained. Important This article refers to Power BI Premium or its capacity subscriptions (P SKUs). Currently, Microsoft is consolidating purchase options and retiring the Power BI Premium per-capacity SKUs. New and existing customers should consider purchasing Fabric capacity subscriptions (F SKUs) instead. For more information, see Important update coming to Power BI Premium licensing and Power BI Premium FAQ . Considerations and key actions Checklist - Considerations and key actions you can take to establish or improve your COE. Define the scope of responsibilities for the COE : Ensure that you're clear on what activities the COE can support. Once the scope of responsibilities is known, identify the skills and competencies required to fulfill those responsibilities. Identify gaps in the ability to execute : Analyze whether the COE has the required systems and infrastructure in place to meet its goals and scope of responsibilities. Determine the best COE structure : Identify which COE structure is most appropriate (centralized, unified, federated, or decentralized). Verify that staffing, roles and responsibilities, and appropriate organizational chart relationships (HR reporting) are in place. Plan for future growth : If you're starting out with a centralized or decentralized COE, consider how you will scale the COE over time by using the unified or federated approach. Plan for any actions that you can take now that'll facilitate future growth. Identify customers : Identify the internal community members, and any external customers, to be served by the COE. Decide how the COE will generally engage with those customers, whether it's a push model, pull model, or both models. Verify the funding model for the COE : Decide whether the COE is purely a cost center with an operating budget, whether it will operate partially as a profit center, and/or whether chargebacks to other business units will be required. Create a communication plan : Create you communications strategy to educate the internal community of users about the services the COE offers, and how to engage with the COE. Create goals and metrics : Determine how you'll measure effectiveness for the COE. Create KPIs (key performance indicators) or OKRs (objectives and key results) to validate that the COE consistently provides value to the user community. Questions to ask Use questions like those found below to assess the effectiveness of a COE. Is there a COE? If so, who is in the COE and what's the structure? If there isn't a COE, is there a central team that performs a similar function? Do data decision makers in the organization understand what a COE does? If there isn't a COE, does the organization aspire to create one? Why or why not? Are there opportunities for federated or decentralized COE models due to a mix of enterprise and departmental solutions? Are there any missing roles and responsibilities from the COE? To what extent does the COE engage with the user community? Do they mentor users? Do they curate a centralized portal? Do they maintain centralized resources? Is the COE recognized in the organization? Does the user community consider them to be credible and helpful? Do business users see central teams as enabling or restricting their work with data? What's the COE funding model? Do COE customers financially contribute in some way to the COE? How consistent and transparent is the COE with their communication? Maturity levels The following maturity levels will help you assess the current state of your COE. Level State of the Center of Excellence 100: Initial • One or more COEs exist, or the activities are performed within the data team, BI team, or IT. There's no clarity on the specific goals nor expectations for responsibilities. • Requests for assistance from the COE are handled in an unplanned manner. 200: Repeatable • The COE is in place with a specific charter to mentor, guide, and educate self-service users. The COE seeks to maximize benefits of self-service approaches to data and BI while reducing the risks. • The goals, scope of responsibilities, staffing, structure, and funding model are established for the COE. 300: Defined • The COE operates with active involvement from all business units in a unified or federated mode. 400: Capable • The goals of the COE align with organizational goals, and they are reassessed regularly. • The COE is well-known throughout the organization, and consistently proves its value to the internal user community. 500: Efficient • Regular reviews of KPIs or OKRs evaluate COE effectiveness in a measurable way. • Agility and implementing continual improvements from lessons learned (including scaling out methods that work) are top priorities for the COE. Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned. (Adobe Stock) By Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 26, 2026, 5 a.m. RELATED ARTICLE Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes Andrew Deck October 17, 2026 Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry. Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic. “We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday. A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences. Meta’s controversial terms October 15 Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say October 17 Legal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changes October 21 U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline October 22 Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites October 26 ★ Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical. October 27 “A gross abuse of Meta’s power”: California senator Adam Schiff tells Meta to scrap its new terms of service October 28 Meta pledges to consult publishers before finalizing its new terms November 5 Meta pulls down controversial terms of service Legal experts and news industry leaders remain skeptical of Meta’s statements. “Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.” “I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.” Thomas Höppner , a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.” The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said. “My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.” News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences. On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day. Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted. A Commission spokesperson said in a statement to Nieman Lab on Friday the the Commission has sent “its first formal requests for information under the AI Act, including to providers that have not published summaries about the data used to train their models.” “The Commission welcomes Meta’s announcement that it has postponed the entry into force of its new commercial terms,” the statement reads. “The Commission is committed to ensuring that Meta’s practices comply in full with all applicable obligations under EU law, including Article 102 TFEU and the Digital Markets Act.” In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms. “The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.” Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.” RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 “What needs to happen next is for the Competition and Markets Authority, and other regulators around the world, to secure clear, public commitments from Meta to abandon the offending elements of the new Terms before they take effect,” Bamber said. That was easier said than done. The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right? (Adobe Stock) By Elizabeth Bromstein Oct. 26, 2026, 11:17 a.m. Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research. But I couldn’t find it. This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about. In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for. I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself. Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from? Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute. Me: Great. Which study? Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research. Me: So where did the number come from? Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense . Me: Does the book contain the original research? Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown. Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell? Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood? A breakthrough! Or so I thought Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy . Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha! I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there. Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book. I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere. Does 75% even make sense? There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job? I asked Kristen Lindquist , a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic. “I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me. There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us. So, what about that breakup? “If you get dumped and you smell some nice cookies, are you going to feel 75% better?” Lindquist said. “Probably not.” When repetition becomes evidence RELATED ARTICLE Repetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate science Yangxueqing Mary Jiang August 12, 2024 There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth. I called Jodi Schneider , an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself. “It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.” Her conclusion: “It’s hard to source.” The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.” This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect : We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true. In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true. It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time. Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity). Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true. Then came AI AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source. “The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.” Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out. When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.) Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign. That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there. I just can’t find it. Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected] . Elizabeth Bromstein is a writer, editor, and perfumer. Do I need to submit both my Masters and Fellowship application by the First Deadline November 13th? Bene Fellowship 2026 Open Call for Applications Deadline Monday, November 30, 2026 - 23:59 ET Programs Climate-Resilient Food Systems Duration 10 weeks to 12 months Topic(s) Development Environment Food and Agriculture Natural Resources Funded by Bene Endowment fund and IDRC Budget Up to ten awards of a maximum of CA$30,000 Point of contact benefellowship@idrc.ca Type Student award Status Open Scope IDRC has helped graduate students undertake research in the field of international development since 1982. The Bene fellowship, a bequest from the estate of John G. Bene, is offered to Canadians and permanent residents of Canada pursuing master’s or doctoral studies at a Canadian university. Candidates should have an academic background that combines an interest in forests (landscape and forest management and restoration, forestry, agroforestry), environment, ecology and food systems, with a social sciences lens (gender and inclusion, Indigenous knowledge and science, biodiversity conservation, governance of nature).   This fellowship aims to facilitate practical field research on gender-responsive integrated forest, landscape and food systems restoration and management including within fire prone, degraded or disputed landscapes. Linking the broader climate-food-inclusivity nexus, it emphasizes nature-based solutions and approaches that have the potential to drive transformative change for smallholder farmers, including youth, women, and Indigenous communities in developing countries. The successful candidate will propose research that benefits less privileged people in developing countries aiming to increase the resilience of individuals and forest/agroforest communities facing difficult contexts and challenges. Note that work focused on genomics and/or genetic modification is not eligible.   Proposals that align with IDRC's REVIVE Initiative on post-fires forest and food restauration and food systems transformation are welcome.     Learn more about John G. Bene.   Eligibility This call is open to Canadians and permanent residents of Canada pursuing master’s or doctoral studies at a Canadian university. The award under this call will cover costs of field research conducted for a master’s thesis or doctoral dissertation in one or more countries of the Global South.
